dances.title: Crossing the Country
dances.callingNotes:
An accidental variation on Further and More, by Lisa
Greenleaf, “choreographed” via process of elimination
and the search-by-phrase tool in Caller’s Box. Initially,
I assumed this dance was Legends of the Hidden Temple,
by Dugan Murphy, having plugged in all of the figures
except for the actual Rory O’More slides.

As it turns out, it’s an exact match of Dugan’s dance if
you disregard the quintuple progression. Dugan’s figures
aren’t published on Caller’s Box and I didn’t bother to
do my research, telling an entire hall of dancers in
Portland, ME that this was Dugan’s dance (sorry Lisa!).

This is also a fixed version of Destiny by Don Flaherty,
so feel free to insert my usual noises about dance
originality and novel choreography here: [ … ]

dances.title: Really Spicy Kimchi

figures.note: Modified right and left through with partner

dances.callingNotes:
Inspired by Maggie’s Hobby by Bob Dalsemer. Having
danced the original at NW Folklife in 2024, we wanted to
address the somewhat tricky pass-through-circle left
progression and sneak in a neighbor swing, if possible.

The caller unintentionally had dancers turn alone before
returning up the hall during the first walk-through of
Maggie’s, but putting the larks in the center of the wave
set things up for a neat little swing through in the B2.

dances.callingNotes:
If you’ve run out of figures from contra dancing to use in
your choreography, it never hurts to shamelessly lift
your novelty from Modern Western Squares —

Crossover Circulate: Dancers facing out in the waves
trade the wave with each other to face in. Dancers facing
into the set cross on the diagonal, passing by the left or
right, as appropriate, to face out in new short waves.

dances.title: Thirty Minute Lunch

params.text: petronella left - move clockwise one place around ring

dances.callingNotes:
Often, in my case, the dance writing process begins with
a measure of (lovingly) blatant theft. In that vein, this
dance is a synthesis of several other excellent dances:

First is Aioli by Will Mentor, borrowing a delightfully
simple A1 progression that fits and flows beautifully.

The B1 comes from Renewed Joy by Rachel Fifer, the one
contra dance I would bring with me on a deserted island.

Finally, the B2 is drawn from an English country dance
written for Turning of the Hour by Rachel Bell. When I
first danced it, I spent the next month thinking about
very little else…until eventually this dance was written.

dances.title: All Along the Equinox
dances.callingNotes:
Chevron: a “meanwhile” figure ending with neighbors
having traded places on the side—robins pass right
shoulders across to trade places and continue facing out
of the set, then larks cast over their right shoulder into
their neighbor’s place while the robins back up to fill the
space left by the lark. Taking hands across as robins back
up, partners then flow directly into the half poussette.

The A2 pass through and turn is towards partners, like a
hands-free roll away. Caution dancers to take their time
dancing the chevron and the poussette, or they’ll arrive
at the partner swing with far too much time to spare.

Inspired by Companions, Victor Skowronski (2003).

dances.title: Helgesson Hall

figures.note: to a line of four, ones splitting twos

dances.callingNotes:
The astute archivist among you may notice that this
dance is a repeat from the first volume of my dances.

Perhaps some advice for an aspiring choreographer—
If you write a dance for someone and, having
danced it, they tell you that they liked what you wrote
for them, you might consider not making changes to
that dance prior to publication without telling them.

You might also consider not misspelling their name
when you put it in your book…or leaving it misspelled
in the second edition of that same book. Just a thought.
(Sorry Frannie)

dances.title: Hey for Thee
dances.callingNotes:
I can’t personally take credit for the trademark figure in
this dance—Penelope Weinberger came up with this
swing/orbit combination for her dance Exorbitant.

Alternating, one couple balances across, about to swing
their partner. Other couples balance right hands while
identifying the couple to their own right (this is always
current neighbors for larks & next neighbors for robins).

While half the couples swing in the center, the other half
pull by to orbit once around their identified neighbors,
passing their shadow by the right at the halfway point.
All end where they began the B2, facing new neighbors.

dances.title: Spicy Snacks
dances.callingNotes:
A few years ago, I visited a friend to borrow a button
accordion that I would later go on to purchase, hooked
on the traditional music of Newfoundland. They escorted
me down into their basement, gesturing grandly to a wall
stacked floor-to-ceiling with accordions and string
instruments, and said “welcome, to the Arsenal.”

I originally sent a screenshot of this dance to Will Mentor
with the heading “Eg -”, still brainstorming the idea and
sending this along as an example. To this day, I believe
Will still has “AKA ‘Eg’” written as the title for this dance.
